planting.note: Grow in pure sphagnum moss or a peat/sand carnivorous plant mix in bright light, watering only with distilled or rain water; expect unusually large traps ringed with long interlocking spines. Needs a cool winter dormancy.

directions: This selection produces unusually large traps ringed with long, closely interlocking marginal spines that give the open trap a menacing, tooth-filled appearance. Traps color to a deep interior red under strong light and consistently outgrow those of the standard wild-type plant. Divide congested rosettes in early spring to multiply the clone true to type, since seed-grown offspring will not retain the long-spine trait. Keep the crown just above the soil surface to prevent rot during humid summer growth.

common_name: Royal Red Venus Flytrap (Deep Burgundy Cultivar)

planting.note: Grow in pure sphagnum moss or a peat/sand carnivorous plant mix in bright light, watering only with distilled or rain water; full sun deepens the uniform burgundy coloration. Needs a cool winter dormancy.

directions: This cultivar was selected for its uniformly deep burgundy-red coloration that develops across the entire trap and petiole rather than fading toward the leaf base as in many red forms. Full, unfiltered sun intensifies the color within a few weeks of new growth. Because seedlings segregate widely in color intensity, only divisions of the original clone are sold true to name. Reduce winter feeding and allow the rosette to go dormant to maintain vigor for the following growing season.

planting.note: Grow in pure sphagnum moss or a peat/sand carnivorous plant mix in bright light, watering only with distilled or rain water; the long, blade-like marginal teeth need strong light to stay rigid. Needs a cool winter dormancy.

directions: Sawtooth is distinguished by unusually long, narrow marginal teeth that overlap tightly when the trap closes, resembling the blade of a saw more than the typical cilia of the species. The extended teeth make the closed trap noticeably shaggy in outline compared with standard clones. Propagate by leaf-pulling or rhizome division to preserve the tooth pattern, since it does not breed reliably true from seed. Bright light keeps the teeth rigid and well colored rather than lax and pale.

common_name: Cupped Trap Venus Flytrap (Bowl-Shaped Lobe Cultivar)

planting.note: Grow in pure sphagnum moss or a peat/sand carnivorous plant mix in bright light, watering only with distilled or rain water; young traps curl into a bowl shape rather than lying flat. Needs a cool winter dormancy.

directions: Rather than closing flat, the trap lobes of this cultivar curl inward to form a distinct bowl or cup shape even before a trigger hair is touched. The cupping is most pronounced on young, vigorously growing traps and becomes less obvious as leaves age. Because the trait is a growth-form mutation rather than a color trait, growers confirm true stock by observing several successive flushes of new traps. Divide clumps every couple of years to keep the cupped growth habit expressing strongly.

common_name: Low Giant Venus Flytrap (Compact Rosette Giant-Trap Cultivar)

planting.note: Grow in pure sphagnum moss or a peat/sand carnivorous plant mix in bright light, watering only with distilled or rain water; the flat, spreading rosette carries traps as large as upright giant cultivars. Needs a cool winter dormancy.

directions: Low Giant combines an unusually flat, ground-hugging rosette with traps that grow as large as those of upright giant cultivars, producing a wide, dense mat of foliage. The low growth habit makes it less prone to wind or watering damage than taller giant clones of similar trap size. Grow in a shallow, wide container to give the spreading rosette room, and divide offsets from the base once the pot becomes crowded. Consistent bright light is needed to keep the flattened growth form from stretching upward.

planting.note: Grow in pure sphagnum moss or a peat/sand carnivorous plant mix in bright light, watering only with distilled or rain water; marginal spines are shortened and fewer than on typical clones. Needs a cool winter dormancy.

directions: Microdent carries a mutation that shortens and reduces the number of the marginal spines lining each trap, giving the lobe edges a smoother, less bristly appearance than typical clones. The trait is most visible on mature traps produced after the plant has been growing under strong light for a full season. Because the reduced-tooth form is a stable but non-seed-true mutation, only division propagates it reliably. Otherwise it is grown under the same bright, moist, low-nutrient conditions as any other flytrap cultivar.

common_name: Slack's Giant Venus Flytrap (Historic Giant-Trap Cultivar)

planting.note: Grow in pure sphagnum moss or a peat/sand carnivorous plant mix in bright light, watering only with distilled or rain water; one of the oldest named giant-trap clones still in cultivation. Needs a cool winter dormancy.

directions: One of the oldest named giant-trap selections in cultivation, this clone was popularized by British carnivorous-plant author Adrian Slack and has remained in circulation among collectors for decades. Its traps regularly exceed the size of unselected wild-type plants while retaining typical green-and-red coloration. Because it has been divided and passed along for so long, plants sold under this name can vary somewhat in vigor depending on the stock's history. Provide the same nutrient-poor, wet, sunny conditions as other flytraps, and divide the rhizome in early spring to bulk up a clump.
sources: Adrian Slack, "Insect-Eating Plants and How to Grow Them"

common_name: Korean Melody Shark Venus Flytrap (Red Shark-Tooth Cultivar)

planting.note: Grow in pure sphagnum moss or a peat/sand carnivorous plant mix in bright light, watering only with distilled or rain water; cool nights during active growth deepen the red trap color. Needs a cool winter dormancy.

directions: This cultivar, developed through Korean tissue-culture breeding programs, pairs a deep red trap interior with short, blunt marginal spines that give the trap edge a stubby, shark-tooth silhouette distinct from the long cilia of wild-type plants. Color intensifies with strong light and cool night temperatures during active growth. Because tissue-cultured stock can vary between labs, plants sold under this name occasionally show minor differences in tooth length or color depth. Divide the rhizome once several growing points have formed to produce identical offsets.

common_name: Wacky Traps Venus Flytrap (Contorted-Trap Novelty Cultivar)

planting.note: Grow in pure sphagnum moss or a peat/sand carnivorous plant mix in bright light, watering only with distilled or rain water; some traps emerge twisted or asymmetrical instead of paired evenly. Needs a cool winter dormancy.

directions: Wacky Traps produces irregularly twisted, folded, or asymmetrical trap lobes on at least some of its leaves, a novelty growth pattern that distinguishes it from the paired, symmetrical traps of typical plants. Not every trap on the plant shows the contortion, and the degree of twisting can vary between growing seasons. The unusual form is maintained only through division, since seedlings do not reliably inherit it. Otherwise the plant is no more demanding than a standard flytrap, needing the same bright light and mineral-free water.

common_name: Red Piranha Venus Flytrap (All-Red Interior Cultivar)

planting.note: Grow in pure sphagnum moss or a peat/sand carnivorous plant mix in bright light, watering only with distilled or rain water; young traps flush an intense near-black red across the inner lobe. Needs a cool winter dormancy.

directions: Red Piranha was selected for traps that flush a deep, almost black-red across the entire inner lobe surface under bright light, more intensely and uniformly than many other red cultivars. The dark coloration is most dramatic on young, actively snapping traps and can fade somewhat as leaves mature. It is widely distributed through tissue culture, so plants sold under this name are usually true to the clone, though color depth still depends heavily on light intensity. Grow under strong sun and allow a cool dormant rest each winter to keep the plant vigorous for the next season's color.

planting.note: Grow in pure sphagnum moss or a peat/sand carnivorous plant mix in bright light, watering only with distilled or rain water; mature traps open unusually wide at the hinge. Needs a cool winter dormancy.

directions: Big Mouth is named for traps that open unusually wide at the hinge, giving each lobe pair a broader gape than the more triangular traps of standard plants. The wide-opening trap form is most visible on the largest, most mature leaves produced during peak summer growth. Because the wide-gape trait is propagated only through division of the original clone, seed-grown plants will not display it reliably. Bright light and steady moisture keep trap production high enough to show the distinctive wide mouth shape repeatedly through the season.
